newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: OPINION - NO QUICK FIX AT ZAMBIA POLL - BY T.HAWKINS.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - NO QUICK FIX AT ZAMBIA POLL - BY T.HAWKINS.

text.p: By Tony Hawkins, Professor of Business Studies at The University of Zimbabwe

If the official numbers are right, Zambians are worse off today than they were when they elected President Frederick Chiluba and his ruling Movement for Multi-Party Democracy (MMD) to office five years ago.

GDP has fallen in three of the last four years, but should grow some 3.5 to 4.0 percent in 1996. Even so, real per capita incomes now are approximately 12 percnet lower than they were when the voters threw out former President Kenneth Kaunda and his United National Independence Party (UNIP), in October 1991.

As always, such figures, on their own, present an incomplete picture. Whatever its failings - and they are many - the Chiluba administration has tackled economic reform with greater vigour and commitment than the Kaunda government, which presided over two decades of stagnation and decline.
Although it may not mean much, Zambia has sub-Saharan Africa's most successful privatisation programme.
Tax rates have been cut, inflation - while still a major problem - was down to 45 percent in September from 93 percent in 1991 and 192 percent in 1992.
Real interest rates are positive, exchange controls have been lifted, domestic markets deregulated and the economy opened up to global competition.
And yet, sadly, the government has little to show for its efforts.

In campaigning for votes for the November 18 parliamentary and presidential elections, ministers cannot claim to have turned the economy around. They can blame adverse external conditions - especially drought and, recently, a depressed copper price - as well as the sheer impossibility of transforming a seriously-rundown economy in a so short period of only five years.
Whether the electorate will be convinced remains to be seen.
The reality is that a return to the muddled and unsuccessful, if well-intentioned, policies of ex-president Kaunda is not on the cards.

Not only is the former president boycotting the poll, but his policies of nationalisation and "humanism" are now so thoroughly discredited, that no politician who campaigns on such a platform could hope to win.
A major irony is the standoff between the donor community which has strongly supported Chiluba's reforms and the government.
The dispute is over governance rather than economic policy, with the donors critical of the recent constitutional amendment that excludes Kaunda from contesting the poll on the most spurious grounds.
They are dissatisfied, too, with Chiluba's failure to stamp out corruption, while believing that privatisation should have proceeded faster than it has.

And yet, few - if any - in the donor, diplomatic, business communities can see a viable alternative to the present government. In 27 years at the helm, Kaunda did enormous damage to what could have been one of Africa's more successful economies.
Zambia has enormous agricultural, as well mineral, potential, yet this is not being exploited effectively.
It should have a vibrant tourist sector but a ramshackle infrastructure and inadequate facilities preclude it from competing successfully with neighbouring Zimbabwe, Kenya or even Tanzania.
So long as the government sticks to the narrow, difficult road of IMF/World Bank sponsored economic reform, the prospects for exploiting this potential must improve.

The irony then is that a donor community anxious to see reform succeed should have frozen, or threatened to freeze, non-humanitarian assistance to Lusaka because of "governance" shortcomings. If, as seems probable, Mr Chiluba wins on November 18, albeit in a very low turnout, what then?
Will the donors maintain their ban on the grounds that the elections failed to pass the "free and fair" litmus test, and in the process undermine the reforms implemented so far?

It makes little sense to demand fresh elections, thereby perpetuating investor and business uncertainty and damaging the economy. And if free and fair elections are really what matters, then surely there is a number of other countries, including Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania and Zimbabwe, where a similar rule-of-thumb ought to have been applied.

None of this is to say that the donors are wrong to demand the good governance that is a pre-requisite for successful economic reform. But it does raise an awkward question - one that won't go away. If governments are meeting their IMF benchmarks and donor conditionalities on the economic front, should the donors turn a blind eye to what is happening politically?
In committing himself to a frontal attack on corruption, World Bank president James Wolfenden has answered that question squarely.

The test will come - as in Zambia - when the aid community has to choose between the tantalisingly elusive prospects of economic success, which must be its prime target, and the difficult-to-measure ideal of good governance.
Whatever Mr Wolfenden's priorities, when the chips are down, economic success is likely to be the decisive yardstick.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
